description: A fine-textured, pinkish to reddish-brown West African hardwood, sometimes used as a stand-in for cherry or mahogany. Used for furniture, veneers, panelling, flooring, doors, and boats.

hazards.summary: A cabinet maker's asthma was confirmed by specific challenge with an extract of makore dust, which produced both an immediate and a delayed reaction. No IgE mechanism was found, and the paper refers to the wood as African cherry (makore).
HSE lists dermatitis among reported effects of makore. The wood contains a quinone that sensitized guinea pigs in laboratory tests.
HSE lists irritation of the nose, throat and airways from makore dust.
HSE also lists effects on the nervous system and blood from makore. No primary report describing these effects was found during this review.
IARC classifies all wood dust as carcinogenic to humans, chiefly through cancers of the nose and sinuses. This applies to makore dust as it does to any other wood.

known_compounds.name: 2,6-dimethoxy-1,4-benzoquinone
known_compounds.role: quinone contact sensitizer found in makore and many other woods

related_species_note: Not the same as Prunus africana, which is also called African cherry. See notes_internal.
image_prompt: Photorealistic studio photograph of a freshly planed makore (Tieghemella heckelii) board, shot at a low three-quarter angle so the face grain fills most of the frame. Even pinkish-brown to deep reddish-brown heartwood with a narrow band of paler pinkish-grey sapwood along one edge. Straight to slightly interlocked grain with occasional mottled or moire figure, fine uniform texture, and a soft lustrous sheen. Soft diffused daylight from upper left, gentle falloff, neutral warm-grey seamless background, shallow depth of field with the near edge tack-sharp. No text, no logos, no hands, no tools, no finish or varnish, natural unfinished wood. Wide 1200x630 composition (1.91:1) with the board centered and margin on both sides for cropping.
image_alt: Planed board of makore with fine-textured pinkish to reddish-brown heartwood and a narrow pale sapwood edge.
notes_internal: Name conflict resolved: SENSOR-2017 maps Obata-2000's 'makore' to Prunus africana. The Obata paper (full text read) never gives a binomial, calls the wood 'African cherry (Makore)', and uses Hausen's chapter titled 'Tieghemella heckelii, Makore' (Woods Injurious to Human Health, 1981, pp 89-91) as its background reference, plus Sandermann & Barghoorn 1955 on 'Makore- und Peroba-Holz'. Makore is the standard trade name for T. heckelii; Prunus africana is not a common furniture timber. Conclusion: tested wood was almost certainly T. heckelii, but it was identified by trade name only (no botanical verification of the sample). Hausen-1978 abstract names Makore without a binomial.
